"The first few days of a closure are a scheduling problem. After that, it's a market problem," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. replacement.dek: The Port of Corpus Christi's lifeline is still open, for now. Here is what the Coast Guard's first storm condition means for the port, its workers and the relief cargo waiting to come in.
body: As of Saturday, the channel that carries about half of the nation's crude exports is still open, but the clock is running.

With Hurricane Rafael approaching, the Coast Guard has set Port Condition X-Ray for the Port of Corpus Christi, meaning gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours. Ships in port have been told to make departure plans or ask the Coast Guard for permission to stay, and the crude docks are slowing their loading. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement has been postponed.

"Safety comes first, and we'll follow the Coast Guard's lead on the channel," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "This port has come back from storms before, and it will again. Our job right now is to secure the docks and be ready for the day after."

The slowdown strains the chain the Ledger described last month: pipeline to tank farm, tank farm to tanker, tanker to anchorage, anchorage to the Gulf. Tankers that would have loaded this week are waiting, and should the channel close, the queue offshore will be the first thing to clear when it reopens.

It also puts relief cargo at risk. Forty relief containers booked on the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider, as the Ledger reported Thursday, have not reached port, and a closure would leave them waiting like every other ship.

"If the channel closes, nothing moves through it, relief or crude," said Terry Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, the freight forwarder handling the booking. "We'll be ready when it opens. The trucks are lined up on paper. They just need a ship at a dock."

For dock workers, line handlers, pilots and tug crews, a storm slowdown means idle time and storm preparation instead of paid shifts. For businesses that depend on port traffic, it means a pause of unknown length.

Salinas would not say whether the port expects to close; port conditions are set by the Coast Guard. Reopening after a storm closure typically follows inspection of the channel and port facilities. The Ledger will report the port's status as it changes.

replacement.headline: Fort Hood brigade's move through Corpus Christi postponed as Coast Guard sets storm condition
replacement.dek: The Army aviation brigade had been scheduled to ship its helicopters and equipment through the port this late summer. A Fort Hood spokesman says the unit will be ready when the port is.
body: On a gray Saturday afternoon, the cargo docks at the Port of Corpus Christi were quiet. The ship channel beyond them was nearly empty. And a move that the Army had planned for months was on hold.

A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement through Corpus Christi has been postponed as Hurricane Rafael approaches, officials said Saturday, the day the Coast Guard set Port Condition X-Ray, warning that gale-force winds are possible within 48 hours. The brigade had been scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer for an overseas rotation.

"Our soldiers are ready to deploy when the port is ready," said Maj. Darnell Price, a public affairs officer at Fort Hood. "The safety of the port, this community and our people comes first. We'll adjust the timeline and keep moving."

Price declined to give a new timeline or to describe where the brigade's equipment is now, consistent with the Army's practice of not detailing unit movements in advance. He described the destination only as an overseas rotation.

As Coastline explained last month, a brigade's port movement is a chain: equipment travels from the home post toward the seaport, is staged and prepared on the docks, and is loaded onto a sealift ship. A postponement means re-sequencing that chain, including ship schedules, staging space and the timing of soldiers' travel. None of that can be finalized until the storm passes and the port is ready to receive the ship.

The Port of Corpus Christi is a designated strategic seaport, sharing its channel between military cargo and one of the busiest crude export operations in the country. The port itself stayed open Saturday, though ocean-going ships had to arrange to leave or win Coast Guard approval to stay, and crude loading was tapering off.

The postponement comes a day after NAS Corpus Christi and NAS Kingsville flew their training aircraft to Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth and Corpus Christi Army Depot halted work to secure helicopters in its hangars. Together, the moves amount to a pause in much of the region's military aviation activity until the storm passes.

For military families, the immediate question is the storm, not the deployment. Price said Fort Hood would share updates on the brigade's movement when it could. Coastline Public Radio will report them when they are released.

body: The drill whines. The plywood goes up. Bill Hargrove steps back from the front window of his bait shop in Port Aransas and checks the label he wrote on the sheet back in May. Front left. Right where it belongs.

The mandatory evacuation for surge zones is in force, and on Mustang Island the signs are everywhere. Shops along the main drag are boarded. The beach is empty. The ship channel past the jetties is now closed to inbound ships.

"You cut it in May so you don't have to think in September," says Hargrove, 64. He has ridden out two hurricanes on the island. Asked whether he will make it three, he squints at the sky. "Ask me tomorrow."
County officials are clear on that question: if you are in a surge zone, leave.
Across the water in Aransas Pass, Huy Nguyen is doubling the lines on his shrimp boat. Extra fenders. Chafe gear where the lines cross the dock. He checks every knot twice.
"Boat I can fix," says Nguyen, 51. "Me, not so easy." He says he will leave once the boat is secure.
Up and down the harbor, crews do the same. Lines get doubled. Gear comes off decks. Engines get one last look.
Shelters are open inland. County buses are picking up residents who do not have cars. If you are on the islands or near the bays and have not left, now is the time.
Harborline 6 will be on the coast through the storm, from a safe location.

replacement.dek: Forecasters call the storm surge life-threatening. Anyone in a surge zone who has not left should leave now.
body: A hurricane warning issued Sunday remains in effect for the Coastal Bend. Hurricane Rafael is forecast to make landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 storm, pushing 9 to 12 feet of storm surge, the National Weather Service said Monday.

"Nine to 12 feet of water is not a flood you wade through. In a lot of homes near the bays, that's water over your head, and in some, over the roofline," said Ben Arceneaux, a meteorologist with the weather service office in Corpus Christi. "If you've been told to leave, leave now. Not after lunch. Now."

A warning means hurricane conditions are expected. Tropical-storm-force winds typically arrive hours before a hurricane's center, and once they do, driving becomes dangerous and emergency crews may not be able to reach people. That shortens the window to evacuate more than many people expect.

Storm surge is the greatest threat. Surge is seawater pushed ashore by a storm's winds, and on the Coastal Bend the bays shape where it goes. Water driven through the passes and into Corpus Christi Bay and Nueces Bay piles up against shorelines that have nowhere to send it. When surge arrives on top of the tide, it reaches higher still.
The region is already wet. Tropical moisture that streamed ahead of Rafael saturated soils last week and pushed the Nueces River up at Calallen. More heavy rain will run off fast.

A mandatory evacuation for surge zones has been in effect since Sunday. Shelters are open inland, and county buses are picking up residents without cars. The Port of Corpus Christi has been closed to inbound ships since Sunday, and the region's Navy air stations flew their training aircraft to Fort Worth on Friday.

If you live outside a surge zone and are staying, forecasters recommend sheltering in a sturdy building, in an interior room away from windows on the lowest floor that is not at risk of flooding. Fill bathtubs and containers with water for washing. Charge everything. Keep a battery radio on.
"People think the danger is the wind they can hear," Arceneaux said. "The danger is the water they can't see coming in the dark."
The Ledger will update this story throughout the day and night.

Whether to keep a laden ship at a protected berth or send it to sea ahead of a hurricane is a judgment that port operators and the Coast Guard make storm by storm, weighing the danger of sailing into heavy weather against the risk of riding it out beside a dock.
The Coast Guard said the terminal's operator, which it did not identify Tuesday, had reported a discharge from two vessels at its berth and was working with authorities.

body: About 9,000 barrels of crude oil spilled from two tankers moored in Corpus Christi's Inner Harbor as Hurricane Rafael arrived, the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office said Wednesday as they formed a Unified Command to lead the response.

"Our priorities are the safety of the public and our responders, and protecting the most sensitive shoreline," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a Coast Guard spokesperson. "We will put crews on the water as soon as the winds allow it. We are not there yet." The cause of the release remains under investigation, she said.
The Unified Command has requested Navy salvage equipment to support the response, Ruiz said. She did not say what equipment had been requested or when it would arrive.

Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the General Land Office's oil spill program, said the agency would focus first on keeping oil out of marshes and other sensitive areas once boats and boom can go out. "Shoreline is where a spill gets slow and expensive," Whitaker said. "The sooner we get boom in the water, the more shoreline we save."

Rendal Terminals said it was cooperating fully with the Unified Command. Anchorage: Ships that rode out the storm at sea have been returning since Friday to the anchorage east of Port Aransas to wait for the channel. Count at the Sept. 12 inbound closure: 14 vessels. No reopening timeline has been issued.

replacement.headline: Federal disaster declaration for Texas coast covers cleanup; aid to households awaits damage counts

body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — A federal major disaster declaration for three Texas counties battered by Hurricane Rafael will help pay for debris removal and emergency protective measures, but aid to individual households will have to wait for damage assessments now under way, the Federal Emergency Management Agency said Saturday.

The declaration covers Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties, where Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island near Port Aransas early Tuesday as a Category 3 hurricane, pushing about 11 feet of storm surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays. Satellite imagery showed about 43 square miles flooded across the three counties.

"This declaration lets the federal government start sharing the cost of the work that has to happen right now: clearing roads, hauling debris, protecting lives and property," said Rachel Ostrander, an external affairs officer for FEMA Region 6. "Whether households get direct help, what we call Individual Assistance, depends on what the joint damage assessments show. Those teams are out now."

Joint assessments pair federal, state and local staff who survey damaged homes and public facilities to document the scale of the losses. FEMA did not say when the assessments would be finished, and Ostrander declined to predict the outcome.

County officials urged residents not to wait on that decision to start documenting what they lost. "Take pictures before you tear anything out, and keep every receipt," said Dwayne Pruitt, public information officer for the Nueces County Office of Emergency Management. "If household aid comes, you'll be glad you did. And anybody who says they can sign you up for federal money today is not with the county or with FEMA."

The storm left more than flooded homes. Two moored tankers at an Inner Harbor terminal released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude, and on Saturday the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting and Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. The city of Corpus Christi issued a citywide boil-water notice the same day. The port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, remains closed.

replacement.headline: Cargo-systems vendor says its remote-maintenance credentials were misused

Dana Feld of Northlight Threat Lab said the posts, which spread in the days after Rafael made landfall near Port Aransas as a Category 3 hurricane on Sept. 14, repeatedly directed users to aid-help-portal.example, a site made to resemble a legitimate aid portal.

"The pattern is the point," Feld said in an interview. "You have dozens of accounts acting in step, hitting the same emotional notes, and all roads lead to the same fake site. That isn't organic outrage. It's organized."

Feld declined to say who may be behind the accounts. "Governments attribute. Researchers describe," she said. "I can tell you how it works. I'm not going to tell you who until someone with the evidence and the authority says so."

replacement.headline: Analysis: What Rafael has cost the Coastal Bend so far, by the numbers that are public
replacement.dek: Four weeks after landfall, there is no official dollar estimate of the storm's damage. But the public figures already show where the region's economy is hurting, and for how long.
body: There is no official price tag yet on Hurricane Rafael, and there won't be for months. But four weeks after the storm came ashore on Mustang Island, the public numbers already show where the Coastal Bend economy is hurting, and for how long.

The port. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed to all traffic since Sept. 13, the day before landfall, and crude exports have been halted since the port shut to inbound ships a day earlier. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, by analysts' estimates. That means a month of the region's biggest export business on hold, along with the pilots, tug crews, terminal workers and truckers who depend on it.

"Every week the channel is closed is a week of revenue that doesn't come back," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Buyers find other barrels. Some of that business returns when the channel opens, but the lost weeks are lost."

The bays. Fishing and shellfish harvesting have been closed in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays since Sept. 18, after oil from the Inner Harbor spill, an estimated 9,000 barrels, spread across about 33 square miles of water. Texas Parks and Wildlife extended its fishing closure Oct. 5, and the state health department's shellfish closure stands. Shrimpers, guides and bait shops are absorbing the loss with no reopening date.

The water. The citywide boil-water notice has been in effect since Sept. 18, and replacement parts for the water plant's damaged pumps are delayed. Restaurants, coffee shops, child care centers and any business that runs on tap water are paying for workarounds: bottled water, ice and extra labor.

The cleanup. Two emergency contracts have entered the public record: Nueces County's $14.2 million sole-source debris removal contract with Vantorra Restoration LLC, and a $2.1 million federal emergency fuel contract for NAS Corpus Christi with Quellmar Fuel Partners. Those are costs to taxpayers, and they also put crews and trucks to work.

The land. About 43 square miles across Nueces, San Patricio and Aransas counties flooded, according to satellite imagery. Every flooded home is a repair bill, and for many families, a gap between what insurance pays and what rebuilding costs.

The strain. At the peak, 911 calls hit about 2,900 a day, nearly ten times normal, and emergency room visits for stomach illness ran about 180% above normal. Those numbers carry no dollar sign, but they show up later as overtime, missed work and medical bills.

body: It's been almost a month since Hurricane Rafael came ashore on Mustang Island on Sept. 14. Here's where things stand as of Wednesday.

Water: STILL BOIL. The Sept. 18 citywide boil-water notice has not been lifted. Replacement parts for the O.N. Stevens plant's damaged pumps are delayed because the supplier's local warehouse flooded, and they're shipping from out of state. No date has been set to lift the notice.
Stomach illness: EASING. ER visits eased in late September after a surge. Keep up the handwashing, with soap and boiled or bottled water.

Bay fishing: CLOSED. Texas Parks and Wildlife extended its fishing closure in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays on Oct. 5, and the state health department's shellfish closure stays in place. Don't fish or harvest there, and avoid any oil on shorelines.
Ship channel: CLOSED. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed since Sept. 13, and crude exports are halted. No reopening date has been announced.

Spill investigation: ONGOING. The Coast Guard says investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of the two tankers involved in the spill. A maintenance vendor says its remote-maintenance credentials were misused and that it revoked all remote access.
Debris: CONTRACT AWARDED. Nueces County awarded a $14.2 million emergency debris contract. Sort piles at the curb, out of the street, and check county channels for routes.
Scams: WATCH OUT. A researcher tied post-storm rumor posts to a lookalike aid site, aid-help-portal.example, also used in phishing emails. Don't click it.

"We are ready when the Coast Guard is," port spokesperson Javier Salinas said. "Our job is to have berths, pilots and terminals lined up so the minute the channel opens, ships move. That work is happening now."

Salinas declined to give a reopening date, noting that port conditions are set by the Coast Guard, which has said the channel will reopen when it is safe for traffic. Spill response continues in the Inner Harbor and the bays, where about 9,000 barrels released by two moored tankers spread across about 33 square miles after the storm.

Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics, said traders are focused on what comes after the reopening as much as on the reopening itself. "The first day isn't the story. The story is how fast the backlog clears," she said. "You've got ships that have been waiting offshore and buyers who have been sourcing elsewhere for a month. It will take time to get back to rhythm."

Holloway said the Coast Guard's investigation into possible unauthorized remote access to the cargo systems of the two tankers is also on traders' minds. "Nobody's pricing it in yet," she said. "But everyone's asking their own terminals what's connected to what."

Two laden tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, remained moored at the Rendal Terminals berth in the Inner Harbor with Coast Guard approval.

replacement.headline: Fishing vessel's identity broadcast off Port Aransas while it reported a position 600 nm away
replacement.dek: Public AIS data show FV Pelican Ridge's identity transmitting off Port Aransas on the night of Oct. 14-15 while the vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. An analyst calls it consistent with identity spoofing.
body: Public Automatic Identification System data show the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge broadcasting off Port Aransas on the night of Oct. 14-15, while the same vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away, according to an analysis by independent maritime security analyst Ian McCready.

McCready, a former Coast Guard watchstander who reviews public AIS feeds for anomalies, said both tracks cannot belong to one hull. "A vessel can't be in two places 600 nautical miles apart at the same time," he said. "When one identity shows up in both, the pattern is consistent with identity spoofing. Something off Port Aransas was transmitting an identity that wasn't its own."

AIS transponders broadcast a vessel's identity, position, course and speed over VHF radio. Shore stations and satellites collect the messages, and traffic services, port operators and other ships use them to build a picture of who is where. The system reports what the transmitter tells it. "AIS is a self-report," McCready said. "It's very good at telling you what a ship says about itself. On its own, it can't tell you whether that's true."

McCready cautioned against conclusions beyond the data. "I can tell you the tracks are inconsistent and that the inconsistency fits spoofing," he said. "I can't tell you what vessel was transmitting or why. I'd want radar or imagery before I said anything more."
Gulfwater has not independently identified the vessel that was transmitting.

Context: The anchorage off Port Aransas, where tankers routinely wait for berths, has held a queue since ships that put to sea for Hurricane Rafael returned three days after its Sept. 14 landfall; 14 vessels were waiting there when the port closed to inbound traffic two days before the storm. The channel partly reopened Oct. 14, with the inner channel still restricted for spill decontamination.

False identities degrade the traffic picture that mariners and port operators rely on for collision avoidance and vessel management, particularly in a crowded anchorage. Gulfwater will report any official response.

replacement.headline: A boat in two places: what an analyst found in ship-tracking data off Port Aransas
replacement.dek: The identity of a fishing vessel showed up off Port Aransas while the boat itself reported a position some 600 nautical miles away. Here's what that means, and what it doesn't.
body: On the night of Oct. 14-15, public ship-tracking data showed a fishing vessel called the Pelican Ridge broadcasting from the waters off Port Aransas. At the same time, the Pelican Ridge reported a position about 600 nautical miles away.

Both can't be true. Independent maritime security analyst Ian McCready, whose finding was first reported earlier Friday by Henrik Aalto of the Gulfwater Maritime Report, says the pattern is consistent with identity spoofing: a transmitter off Port Aransas using an identity that belonged to a different vessel.

What is the tracking system? It's called AIS, the Automatic Identification System. Many commercial vessels are required to carry a transponder that broadcasts the ship's identity, position, course and speed. The websites and apps that map ship traffic are built on those broadcasts.

How can it be spoofed? "The network trusts the radio," McCready said. "It shows what a transmitter reports. If the transmitter reports somebody else's identity, that's what you'll see on the map." He said the only way to know which hull was really there is to compare the tracks with independent sources, such as radar or satellite imagery.

Why does it matter here? The anchorage off Port Aransas is where tankers routinely wait for berths, and it has been busy since ships came back from sea after Hurricane Rafael; 14 vessels were already waiting offshore when the port closed to inbound traffic before the storm. The channel partly reopened Oct. 14. Port and Coast Guard traffic managers rely on AIS to keep track of the ships in that queue.
What doesn't it tell us? Who, or why. "People want a story," McCready said. "The data only gives you the anomaly. Anything past that is a guess, and I don't guess in public."
No agency has commented publicly on the finding. The Ledger will report any official response.

body: Bill Hargrove's Black Friday sale is written in grease pencil on a sheet of plywood: "LIVE SHRIMP. CHEAP ADVICE. NO REFUNDS ON EITHER."

Hargrove, 64, has sold bait and tackle near the Port Aransas jetties for years. Hurricane Rafael's surge gutted his shop when the storm made landfall on Mustang Island on Sept. 14. Ten weeks later, he is selling out of coolers on the porch while a carpenter works inside.
"Black Friday on the island used to mean the Winter Texans rolling in and buying a rod they didn't need," Hargrove said. "This year it's me, two coolers and whoever's brave enough to drive out."

Rafael hit at the end of a strong summer. Port Aransas businesses reported busy bait shops and charters in August. Then the storm pushed about 11 feet of surge into Corpus Christi and Nueces bays and flooded about 43 square miles across the three coastal counties.

For businesses that depend on the water, the fall brought one closure after another. The ship channel closed Sept. 13 ahead of the storm and only partly reopened Oct. 14. An explosion near the Port Aransas jetties on Oct. 28 closed it again for 14 days, until Nov. 11. And because of the oil spill, fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays have stayed closed since Sept. 18.
The reopened channel matters for the port, where crude exports resumed in mid-November. For a bait shop, Hargrove said, it matters less than people think.
"Big ships don't buy bait," he said. "Fishermen buy bait. And the bays are closed."
Back in Corpus Christi, shoppers lined up before dawn outside big-box stores on South Padre Island Drive. Plenty of carts held more plywood, box fans and extension cords than televisions.
Hargrove said he hopes to have the shop's walls closed in by Christmas, depending on the drywall crew.
"They're on island time, too," he said. "I can't complain. I invented island time."

findings.reason: Channel closed Sept. 13 (PUB-108), not Sept. 11.

replacement.headline: Season-end log: Corpus Christi channel lost weeks to Rafael, spill restrictions and the jetty blast
replacement.dek: The ship channel closed Sept. 13, partly reopened Oct. 14 and closed again for 14 days after the Oct. 28 explosion at the entrance. It has been open since Nov. 11.
body: The Atlantic hurricane season ends today with the Corpus Christi Ship Channel open, after a fall in which the port lost weeks of normal operations to Hurricane Rafael, an Inner Harbor oil spill and an explosion at the entrance channel.
Sept. 11: Coast Guard sets Port Condition X-Ray ahead of Rafael. The port stays open; terminals wind down crude loading.
Sept. 12: Port Condition Yankee closes the port to inbound traffic. Fourteen vessels hold at the offshore anchorage. Crude exports halt.
Sept. 13: Port Condition Zulu closes the channel to all traffic; anchorage ships put to sea. Two laden tankers remain moored at an Inner Harbor terminal with Coast Guard approval.
Sept. 14 to 15: Rafael makes landfall near Port Aransas. Unified Command estimates about 9,000 barrels of crude released from MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay at the Rendal Terminals berth.
Sept. 17: Ships return from sea to the anchorage. The channel stays closed for surveys.

Oct. 14: Channel partly reopens. Inner channel stays restricted for spill decontamination. Anchorage backlog delays relief cargo; MV Gulf Provider berths Oct. 17 with 40 relief containers, about a month late.

Oct. 28: Around 1 a.m., an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties damages the tug and injures two crew. Coast Guard closes the channel. Separately, spill-related inner channel restrictions are lifted as cleanup moves to monitoring.
Oct. 30: Navy says an explosive device caused the blast; a joint Navy-Coast Guard search of the channel is under way.
Nov. 5: Navy teams find a second device near the entrance channel and render it safe.
Nov. 11: Channel reopens after a 14-day closure and full sweep. Exports resume. The next day, a Fort Hood aviation brigade's equipment begins loading onto a sealift ship.

"The channel is open, and we intend to keep it that way," said Javier Salinas, spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "The people who work this port had a hard fall. They've earned a quiet winter."

Open items: Investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the two tankers' cargo-control systems; the maintenance vendor Brightwake Marine Systems has said its remote credentials were misused. The FBI is investigating the blast.

Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a spokesperson for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi, said the service does not comment on open investigations. "Our focus is safe navigation, and the channel is open," she said.

findings.reason: Season log listed a Sept. 11 closure with 14 vessels and the tankers' approval; split into X-Ray Sept. 11 (PUB-020), Yankee Sept. 12 (PUB-107), Zulu Sept. 13 (PUB-108) and ships back at the anchorage Sept. 17 (PUB-109).

replacement.headline: Corpus Christi crude heads into year-end after two fall shutdowns
replacement.dek: Exports from the largest U.S. crude gateway resumed when the ship channel reopened Nov. 11. The bigger question for next year is confidence, not capacity, an analyst says.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from Corpus Christi head into the final weeks of the year with the ship channel open, after a fall in which shipments halted twice: first when the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound traffic Sept. 12 ahead of Hurricane Rafael, and again after an Oct. 28 explosion at the Port Aransas jetties shut it for 14 days.

The port handles an outsized share of U.S. crude exports, about half by analysts' estimates. Before the storm it was loading tankers at near-record pace, and exports hit a monthly high at the end of August.

"Two closures in one quarter, from two completely different causes. That's what buyers will remember," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Exports resumed when the channel reopened. The question now is confidence, not capacity."

The first shutdown outlasted the storm. The channel partly reopened Oct. 14, but spill decontamination kept the inner channel restricted until Oct. 28, and an anchorage backlog delayed cargoes; 14 vessels had queued offshore when the channel first closed. The second halt came Oct. 28, the same day the inner-channel restrictions were lifted, when a blast beside a harbor tug closed the channel again. Navy teams found and rendered safe a second device Nov. 5, and the channel reopened Nov. 11 after a full sweep.
"The channel is open, and we're moving barrels," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi.
Holloway said the open investigation keeps some uncertainty in the market. The FBI is investigating the blast, and officials have not said who was responsible.
"Markets can price a hurricane. There's a century of data on hurricanes," she said. "An open question is harder to price."

findings.reason: First halt dated Sept. 11; exports halted at the inbound closure Sept. 12 (PUB-107).

replacement.headline: Relief forwarder's lesson from Rafael: the cargo was ready, the channel wasn't
replacement.dek: Gulf Relief Logistics booked 40 relief containers before the storm. They landed about a month late. Its regional manager says next season's plan starts at the anchorage.
body: Terry Akins keeps a printout of the MV Gulf Provider's last position taped to the wall of his office near the port. He doesn't need it anymore. He keeps it anyway.

Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, booked 40 relief containers on the cargo ship five days before Hurricane Rafael made landfall. In August, relief agencies had stocked warehouses ahead of peak season, and forwarders like his had signed standby relief contracts. On paper, the Coastal Bend was ready.

Then the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound ships ahead of the storm, with 14 vessels waiting at the offshore anchorage. When the channel partly reopened Oct. 14, the anchorage backlog delayed relief cargo, including Gulf Provider. The ship finally berthed and unloaded its 40 containers Oct. 17, about a month late.

"We had the boxes stuffed, the bookings confirmed, the drayage lined up on the other end. Everything we control, we controlled," Akins said. "What you don't control is the queue at the sea buoy. Fourteen ships ahead of you and a channel that's half open, you're just a line on somebody's lineup."
Relief also came by air. Beginning Oct. 18, 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters landed at NAS Corpus Christi over ten days.
Akins said the holiday lull is when forwarders rewrite their hurricane playbooks, and his rewrite starts with the lesson that a ready cargo is only as fast as the channel.

"Next season I want a plan B that doesn't depend on one channel. Some of it pre-positioned inland before the cone even points at us, some of it ready to move by truck," he said. "Ships are cheap per box. They get real expensive when they're sitting at anchor."

He said he would also push for relief cargo to get clearer priority in any post-storm reopening, though he acknowledged that decision belongs to others. "I'm not the Coast Guard. I just know what a month late looks like to a family waiting on water," he said.
"June comes fast," Akins said. "It always does."

findings.reason: The 14 vessels waited at the anchorage when the port closed to inbound ships (PUB-107); PUB-020 was cited only for that closure.
